Chapter 5: Why Scarcity and Time Preference Matter
Every day, you and I make choices about the future. Some people tuck away a little extra for a rainy day, while others can’t wait to spend what they have the moment it lands in their hands. Now, that’s not just about who’s cautious and who’s carefree—there’s something deeper going on. The kind of money we use actually shapes these decisions in powerful ways.
When money holds its value, saving just makes sense. But if your money loses value quickly, wouldn’t you feel pressured to spend it or even borrow, just to keep up?
There’s a name for this: time preference. It’s really about how much you value what you can have now versus what you might have in the future.
In places where money is solid and reliable, folks tend to have a lower time preference. They’re more willing to wait, to invest in what matters, and to build for the long haul. That’s how businesses grow, families plan, and communities start to thrive.
But when money is easy to print and loses its value fast, time preference jumps. Suddenly, everyone’s thinking about today, not tomorrow. People rack up more debt, and it’s harder to invest in the future.
Picture a small business owner, working late into the night. If she trusts her savings will still be worth something next year, she’ll feel good about reinvesting in her shop, hiring more people, and planning for growth.
But if she’s worried that inflation will eat away at her hard-earned profits, she might spend right away or take risks just to protect what she’s got.
That’s where Bitcoin steps in and changes the rules. With only twenty-one million coins ever, there’s simply no way to make more out of thin air. This built-in scarcity encourages people to think longer term. Saving starts to look attractive again, and suddenly, hard work and patience actually pay off.
But it goes even deeper. When money can’t be manipulated or inflated away, governments and banks have to play by the same rules as everyone else. They can’t just cover up problems with easy money. The discipline of sound money starts to ripple through the whole economy, encouraging responsibility and building trust.
And you know, most people don’t notice these changes right away. They just feel them in little ways—less stress about the future, a greater willingness to save, and a sense that things are a bit more fair.
Over time, those small shifts add up. Societies with sound money tend to be more stable, more innovative, and honestly, more free.
So, the story of Bitcoin? It’s really the story of time preference. It’s about empowering each of us to plan, to save, and to build something lasting. It’s about breaking that old cycle of inflation and short-term thinking. And in a world where money is truly scarce and secure, well, the future just feels a little brighter.
